nodes.summary: For a list $s$ and a list of indices $i_0, i_1, \dots, i_k$, this is the list of length $k$ whose $t$-th entry, for $t < k$, is the length of the longest common prefix of the suffixes of $s$ starting at $i_t$ and at $i_{t+1}$, where the suffix starting at an index at or past the end of $s$ is the empty list. It has one entry per adjacent pair of indices, and it is empty for an empty index list.
nodes.title: Longest-common-prefix lengths of adjacent suffixes

nodes.summary: For a list $s$ over a linearly ordered alphabet, the LCP array of $s$ is the list of longest-common-prefix lengths of adjacent suffixes in suffix-array order: if the suffix array of $s$ is $i_0, i_1, \dots, i_k$, then the LCP array has length $k$ and its $t$-th entry, for $t < k$, is the length of the longest common prefix of the suffixes of $s$ starting at $i_t$ and at $i_{t+1}$. It is empty when $s$ is empty.
nodes.title: The LCP array

nodes.summary: For lists $x$ and $y$, $\mathrm{lcp}(x, y)$ is the length of the longest common prefix of $x$ and $y$: the number of positions, counted from the start, at which $x$ and $y$ agree before they first differ or one of them ends.
nodes.title: Longest common prefix length

nodes.summary: For lists $x$ and $y$, let $\mathrm{lcp}(x, y)$ be the length of the longest common prefix of $x$ and $y$. For every natural number $q$, we have $q \le \mathrm{lcp}(x, y)$ if and only if $q$ is at most the lengths of both $x$ and $y$ and the first $q$ elements of $x$ and of $y$ agree.
nodes.title: Characterization of the longest common prefix length

nodes.summary: If `p` holds on an initial segment of `[lo, hi)` (whenever it holds at `j`, it holds at every `i` with `lo ≤ i ≤ j`), then `lowerBound p lo hi` is the end `k` of that segment: `lo ≤ k ≤ hi`, `p` holds on `[lo, k)` and fails on `[k, hi)`.
nodes.title: Binary search is correct

nodes.summary: At most `⌊log₂ (hi - lo)⌋ + 1` probes, for any predicate.
nodes.title: Binary search is logarithmic

nodes.summary: The number of probes `lowerBound p lo hi` makes.
nodes.title: Number of probes made by the binary search

nodes.summary: Binary search for the boundary of a predicate on `[lo, hi)`: the first index at which `p` is false, assuming `p` holds on an initial segment of `[lo, hi)` (`lowerBound_spec`). Each call probes the midpoint and recurses on one half.
nodes.title: Binary search for the boundary of a predicate

nodes.summary: For a list $s$ over a linearly ordered alphabet, the suffixes of $s$ taken in suffix-array order are sorted lexicographically: whenever an index $i$ comes before an index $j$ in the suffix array of $s$, the suffix of $s$ starting at $i$ is lexicographically less than or equal to the suffix of $s$ starting at $j$.
nodes.title: The suffix array sorts the suffixes

nodes.summary: If `x ≤ y ≤ z` and `P` is a prefix of both `x` and `z`, then `P` is a prefix of `y`.
nodes.title: Prefix classes are lexicographic intervals

nodes.summary: If rows `r₁ ≤ r₂ ≤ r₃` of the suffix array of `s` are in range and the suffixes of rows `r₁` and `r₃` start with `P`, so does the suffix of row `r₂`.
nodes.title: The occurrences of a pattern are contiguous in the suffix array

nodes.summary: The suffix of row `r` of the (precomputed) suffix array `sa` of `s`, truncated to `m` letters: the key compared with the pattern during the search. `sa` is computed once by `saSearch` and passed in, so probes do not rebuild the suffix array.
nodes.title: Truncated suffix of a suffix-array row

nodes.summary: The search returns a genuine interval of rows: `sp ≤ ep ≤ |s|`.
nodes.title: Suffix-array search returns a valid row interval

nodes.summary: A row `r < |s|` lies in `[sp, ep)` exactly when the suffix of row `r` starts with `P`.
nodes.title: Suffix-array search is correct

nodes.summary: Suffix-array search (Manber and Myers 1993): the row interval `[sp, ep)` of the suffixes of `s` that start with `P`, found by two binary searches over the rows `[0, |s|)`. The suffix array is computed once and shared by both searches.
nodes.title: Suffix-array search for a pattern's row interval

nodes.summary: For a list $s$ of length $n$ over a linearly ordered alphabet, the suffix array of $s$ is a permutation of the list $0, 1, \dots, n - 1$ of all indices below $n$.
nodes.title: The suffix array is a permutation of the indices

nodes.summary: For a list $s$ of length $n$ over a linearly ordered alphabet, the suffix array of $s$ is the list of the indices $0, 1, \dots, n - 1$, sorted so that the suffixes of $s$ starting at them appear in lexicographic order.
nodes.title: Suffix array

nodes.summary: For a list $s = (s_0, \dots, s_{n-1})$ over a linearly ordered alphabet and a natural number $i$, the suffix of $s$ at $i$ is the list obtained from $s$ by dropping its first $i$ entries: it is $(s_i, \dots, s_{n-1})$ when $i < n$ and the empty list when $i \ge n$.
nodes.title: Suffix of a list at an index

nodes.summary: For a list $s$ of length $n$ over a linearly ordered alphabet, the list of suffixes of $s$ is the list, for $i = 0, 1, \dots, n$ in this order, of the lists obtained from $s$ by dropping its first $i$ entries. It starts with $s$ itself and ends with the empty list.
nodes.title: Suffixes of a list

nodes.summary: Let $x$ and $y$ be lists and let $\mathrm{lcp}(x, y)$ be the length of their longest common prefix. For every natural number $q \le \mathrm{lcp}(x, y)$, the first $q$ elements of $x$ and of $y$ agree.
nodes.title: Common prefixes of every shorter length

nodes.summary: For lists $x$ and $y$ over a type with decidable equality, let $\operatorname{lcp}(x, y)$ be the length of their longest common prefix. Then the first $\operatorname{lcp}(x, y)$ elements of $x$ and the first $\operatorname{lcp}(x, y)$ elements of $y$ form the same list.
nodes.title: Two lists agree on their longest common prefix

nodes.summary: Truncation is monotone for the lexicographic order: `x ≤ y → x.take m ≤ y.take m`.
nodes.title: Truncation is monotone for the lexicographic order

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
